title: Add Two Numbers
directAnswer: Walk both lists together adding digit-by-digit, exactly like grade-school addition. Keep a running `carry`, compute `sum = l1.val + l2.val + carry`, append `sum % 10` as a new node, and set `carry = sum / 10`. Use a dummy head so you never special-case the first node, and keep looping while either list has digits left OR carry is non-zero — that last condition is what appends the final carry node. O(max(m, n)) time, O(max(m, n)) space for the result list.

remember.pattern: Elementary-school addition over a dummy-headed result list
remember.formula:
dummy = ListNode(0)
curr = dummy
carry = 0
while l1 or l2 or carry:
    x = l1.val if l1 else 0
    y = l2.val if l2 else 0
    s = x + y + carry
    carry = s // 10
    curr.next = ListNode(s % 10)
    curr = curr.next
    l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
    l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
return dummy.next
rules: Digits are stored in **reverse order**, so the list head is the ones place — you add left-to-right and the carry flows naturally forward.
Loop while `l1 OR l2 OR carry` — the **carry term** is what appends the leftover final node (e.g. 5 + 5 = 10 → `[0, 1]`).
Use a **dummy head** node and return `dummy.next`; it removes the 'is this the first node?' special case entirely.
Treat a missing digit as **0** (`l1.val if l1 else 0`) so unequal lengths just work without a separate cleanup loop.
`carry` is always **0 or 1** when adding two base-10 digits (max 9 + 9 + 1 = 19), but write `s // 10` rather than hard-coding it.
Advance `l1`/`l2` **only if they're non-null** — guarding the advance is what lets one list run out before the other.
whenToUse: Adding, subtracting, or multiplying numbers represented as linked-list digits
Any per-element merge of two lists where positions line up and you carry state forward
You need to build a brand-new result list while consuming two inputs in lockstep
Reverse-order digit storage makes least-significant-first processing natural
antiSignals: Digits stored most-significant-first → reverse first, or use a stack (Add Two Numbers II)
Numbers fit in a 64-bit integer and you may convert → just parse, add, rebuild (usually disallowed here)
You must not allocate new nodes → in-place is awkward; this problem expects a fresh list
remember.takeaway: This is the canonical 'build a new list with a dummy head while carrying state forward' problem. The dummy-head + `while a or b or carry` shape recurs in Merge Two Sorted Lists, Add Two Numbers II, and Multiply Strings — master the carry-and-append rhythm once and reuse it everywhere.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can manage a carry cleanly across unequal-length lists and remember to emit the final carry node — plus whether you reach for a dummy head instead of fiddly first-node special-casing.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Stopping the loop when both lists are exhausted but forgetting the leftover carry (so 5 + 5 returns [0] instead of [0, 1]), or crashing on l1.val / l2.val when one list is already null.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Use a dummy head and the single unified `while l1 or l2 or carry` condition so unequal lengths and the final carry all fall out of one loop. Name the grade-school-addition analogy and connect it to Add Two Numbers II and Multiply Strings.

problemStatement:
You are given two **non-empty** linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in ***reverse order***, and each node contains a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list.

You may assume the two numbers do not contain any leading zero, except the number 0 itself.

Because the digits are reversed, the head of each list is the least-significant (ones) digit — which is exactly the digit you add first.
constraints: The number of nodes in each list is in the range [1, 100]
Each number is guaranteed to have no leading zeros, except the number 0 itself
The two lists may have different lengths
understanding: Both numbers arrive least-significant-digit first, so position i of each list is the same place value. We add the two lists like columns in long addition: add the two digits plus any incoming carry, write down the units digit, and carry the tens digit to the next column. The result is also least-significant-first, so we simply append digits as we produce them. The only subtleties are running off the end of the shorter list (treat as 0) and a carry that survives past the last digit (append one more node).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the digits stored most-significant-first or least-significant-first?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Least-significant-first (reversed). That's what makes the carry flow forward as we walk from the head, with no reversal needed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the two lists have different lengths?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. I'll treat a missing digit in the shorter list as 0 so a single loop handles both — no separate cleanup pass.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the final sum produce an extra digit?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — e.g. 5 + 5 = 10, stored as [0, 1]. I keep looping while carry is non-zero so the leftover carry becomes its own node.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to convert the lists to integers, add, then rebuild?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Generally no — the lists can be up to 100 digits, overflowing 64-bit integers. The expected solution adds digit-by-digit directly on the lists.

examples.explanation: 9999999 + 9999 = 10009998. Carry ripples the whole way and spills into a new most-significant node.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Reversed digits + carry-forward is the default. Reverse first only when the input is most-significant-first.

approaches.name: Elementary Addition — Dummy Head + Carry (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it's the intended answer. Phrase it as 'long addition, column by column, carrying forward' rather than 'just loop the lists'.
hints: The digits are reversed, so the heads of both lists are the ones place. That's the column you'd add first by hand. What do you carry into the next column?
Keep a running carry. At each step compute sum = digit1 + digit2 + carry, append sum % 10 as a new node, and set carry = sum / 10. Treat a missing digit as 0.
Loop while EITHER list still has nodes OR carry is non-zero — that last clause appends the final carry node. Use a dummy head and return dummy.next so the first node needs no special case.
approaches.complexityReasoning: We touch each node of the longer list exactly once doing O(1) arithmetic → O(max(m, n)) time. The result list has at most max(m, n) + 1 nodes → O(max(m, n)) space (output only; the carry and pointers are O(1)).
approaches.explanation:
We reproduce exactly what you do when adding two numbers on paper, except the lists hand us the digits in the most convenient order possible: least-significant first. We walk both lists in lockstep, and at each column we add the two digits plus whatever carry came from the previous column.

**Why the reversed order is a gift, not a hassle.** Long addition starts at the ones place and carries leftward into higher place values. Because the lists are stored least-significant-first, the head is the ones place and `next` walks toward higher places — the exact direction the carry needs to flow. So we add front-to-back, append each result digit to the back of the output, and the carry naturally rides forward. If the digits were most-significant-first we'd have to reverse or use stacks; here we get the right direction for free.

**Why the dummy head earns its keep.** Building a list by appending always has an annoying first-node problem: the head pointer is null at the start, so the first append needs different code than the rest. A dummy (sentinel) node sidesteps this entirely. We point `curr` at the dummy, always do `curr.next = new node; curr = curr.next`, and at the end return `dummy.next` — the real first digit. Every iteration uses identical code, which means fewer branches and fewer bugs.

**Why the loop condition is `l1 OR l2 OR carry`.** Three things can keep the addition alive: digits left in `l1`, digits left in `l2`, or a pending `carry`. Using `OR` means the loop runs until *all three* are exhausted. The `carry` term is the subtle one — consider `5 + 5`. Both lists empty after one column, but `carry` is `1`, so the loop runs one more time with both digits treated as `0`, producing the leading `1` node. Drop the `carry` clause and `5 + 5` wrongly returns `[0]` instead of `[0, 1]`.

**Why missing digits become 0.** Unequal lengths are handled with `x = l1.val if l1 else 0`. Once the shorter list runs out, its contribution is `0` for the remaining columns — precisely how you'd pad a shorter number with leading zeros on paper. This collapses what could be three phases (both lists, then leftover of one, then carry) into a single clean loop.
approaches.insight: The entire problem is one loop guarded by `l1 or l2 or carry`, with every awkward case — unequal lengths, the trailing carry, the first-node append — absorbed into that single condition plus a dummy head. When a build-a-list problem tempts you into multiple cleanup loops, look for the unified condition that makes them disappear.

dryRun.intro: carry starts at 0. Each step: sum = x + y + carry, append sum % 10, carry = sum // 10. Dummy head collects the result.

steps.action: l1, l2 empty and carry 0 → stop, return dummy.next

code.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: ListNode, l2: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    curr = dummy
    carry = 0
    while l1 or l2 or carry:
        x = l1.val if l1 else 0
        y = l2.val if l2 else 0
        total = x + y + carry
        carry = total // 10
        curr.next = ListNode(total % 10)
        curr = curr.next
        l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
        l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
    return dummy.next

java.explanation: Sentinel head so the first real digit is appended with the same code as every other digit.
Keep going while either list has digits OR a carry is pending — the carry clause emits the final node.
Missing digit from the shorter list contributes 0, so unequal lengths need no special handling.
Tens digit of the column sum becomes next column's carry (always 0 or 1 here).
Units digit of the column sum is the output digit for this place.
Advance only when non-null so the shorter list can run out without a null-pointer crash.
Skip the sentinel and return the real head of the result list.

python.explanation: Sentinel head; the real result starts at dummy.next.

python.line: while l1 or l2 or carry:
python.explanation: Loop until both lists are consumed AND no carry remains.
Treat an exhausted list as contributing 0 for the remaining columns.
Carry forward the tens digit into the next iteration.
Append the units digit as a new result node.

python.line: l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
python.explanation: Advance l1 only if it still exists, otherwise leave it None.
Return the node after the sentinel — the actual answer.

edgeCases.behavior: Column 0: 5+5=10 → append 0, carry 1. Lists now empty but carry=1 → loop once more, append 1. Result [0, 1]. This is the final-carry case.
Single column 0+0=0, carry 0 → result [0]. Confirms we don't strip a legitimate single zero.

pitfalls: Ending the loop on `l1 != null && l2 != null` instead of `||` — drops the longer list's tail and the final carry.
Forgetting the carry clause in the loop condition — 5 + 5 returns [0] instead of [0, 1].
Reading l1.val / l2.val without a null guard — crashes once the shorter list is exhausted.
Converting the lists to integers and adding — overflows for 100-digit inputs.

commonMistakes: Stopping when both lists end but ignoring a leftover carry — 5 + 5 wrongly yields [0].
Dereferencing l1.val or l2.val after one list is null — null-pointer / attribute error.
Special-casing the first node instead of using a dummy head, leading to tangled head logic.
Trying to parse both lists into integers and sum them — overflows on long inputs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the final carry node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When the last column produces a carry (e.g. the most-significant digits sum to ≥ 10), the leftover carry is a brand-new most-significant digit. If the loop stops as soon as both lists are empty, that digit is lost.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while l1 and l2:
    total = l1.val + l2.val + carry
    carry = total // 10
    curr.next = ListNode(total % 10)
    curr = curr.next
    l1, l2 = l1.next, l2.next
return dummy.next   # drops longer tail AND final carry
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while l1 or l2 or carry:
    x = l1.val if l1 else 0
    y = l2.val if l2 else 0
    total = x + y + carry
    carry = total // 10
    curr.next = ListNode(total % 10)
    curr = curr.next
    l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
    l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
return dummy.next

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Null-pointer on the shorter list
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Once the shorter list is exhausted its pointer is null. Reading .val or advancing it unconditionally crashes. Guard both the read (default to 0) and the advance.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Hand-rolling the first node instead of a dummy head
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without a sentinel you must branch on whether the head exists yet on every append, which is verbose and a frequent source of off-by-one head bugs.
